title: How can one angle of a parallelogram or rhombus give the rest?
description: Four shapes each show one angle. Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add up to one hundred eighty degrees, opposite angles are equal, and the diagonal of a rhombus cuts its corners in half. The four angles of each shape are added to check.
teaching_notes: One idea: use opposite angles, neighbouring angles and the diagonal of a rhombus to find every angle from one. Watch for students who forget that a diagonal cuts a rhombus corner in half, so the given angle is only half of the corner.

source: Figure it Out (parallelograms and rhombuses, question 1)
video_script.why: The child finds all the angles of four shapes from one angle each, using the method of the rhombus example.
video_script.substitution: the book's question with parallelograms PEAR and PQRS and rhombuses UVWX and OIEA
video_script.anchor: four shapes with one angle given each: PEAR with 40, PQRS with 110, UVWX with 30 at V and OIEA with 20 at E
video_script.payoff_line: Each shape has two pairs of equal angles

final_answer.spoken: in the first shape angles E and R are one hundred forty degrees and angle A is forty degrees

never_show: angle V written as 30 degrees alone
maths_rules: PEAR: neighbouring angles add up to 180, so angle E = angle R = 180 - 40 = 140; opposite angle A = angle P = 40
PQRS: angle Q = angle S = 180 - 110 = 70; opposite angle R = angle P = 110
UVWX: diagonal XV cuts angle V and angle X in half, so angle V = 30 + 30 = 60 and angle X = 60; angle U = angle W = 180 - 60 = 120
OIEA: diagonal OE cuts angle E and angle O in half, so angle E = 20 + 20 = 40 and angle O = 40; angle A = angle I = 180 - 40 = 140
each shape: the four angles add up to 360
video_script.design: One idea: neighbouring angles add up to one hundred eighty and opposite angles are equal. Each shape is solved in turn on the board, and the angle sums check them.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; four shapes, each with one angle marked and the other angles as question marks

marks.shapes: the four shapes appear in a row
marks.ask: question marks glow at the missing angles

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about four shapes.
<bookmark mark='shapes'/>Two are parallelograms and two are rhombuses.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Each shows only one angle.
Can we find all the missing angles?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a parallelogram with neighbouring angles joined by a plus sign to a straight angle; a rhombus with its diagonal cutting a corner in half

marks.rule: the neighbouring angles add up to a straight angle
marks.half: the diagonal cuts a corner of the rhombus in half

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>We use the same method as the examples in your book.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add up to one hundred eighty degrees.
<bookmark mark='half'/>A diagonal of a rhombus cuts each corner it touches in half.

beats.on_screen: Given: (i) PEAR, ∠P = 40°; (ii) PQRS, ∠P = 110°; (iii) rhombus UVWX, ∠XVU = 30°; (iv) rhombus OIEA, ∠OEA = 20°

marks.rh: the two rhombus givens are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, P E eigh R is a parallelogram with angle P of forty degrees.
P Q R S has angle P of one hundred ten degrees.
<bookmark mark='rh'/>Rhombus U V W X has angle X V U of thirty degrees.
Rhombus O I E eigh has angle O E eigh of twenty degrees.

beats.on_screen: To find: the remaining angles of each shape
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the remaining angles of each shape.

marks.nb: angle P and angle E light up as neighbours
marks.opp: angle A is matched with angle P

narration: <bookmark mark='nb'/>Step one, in P E eigh R, neighbouring angles add up to one hundred eighty.
<bookmark mark='ev'/>Angle E and angle R are one hundred eighty minus forty, which is one hundred forty degrees.
<bookmark mark='opp'/>Angle eigh is opposite angle P, so it is forty degrees.

marks.nb: angle P and angle Q light up as neighbours
marks.qv: angles Q and S are written
marks.opp: angle R is matched with angle P

narration: <bookmark mark='nb'/>Step two, in P Q R S, neighbouring angles also add up to one hundred eighty.
<bookmark mark='qv'/>Angle Q and angle S are one hundred eighty minus one hundred ten, which is seventy degrees.
<bookmark mark='opp'/>Angle R is opposite angle P, so it is one hundred ten degrees.

beats.on_screen: (iii) UVWX, ∠XVU = 30°: XV cuts ∠V and ∠X in half, so ∠V = ∠X = 30 + 30 = 60°; ∠U = ∠W = 180 − 60 = 120°

marks.vx: angle V and angle X are each made of two thirty degree parts
marks.uw: angles U and W are written

narration: <bookmark mark='diag'/>Step three, the diagonal X V cuts angle V and angle X in half.
<bookmark mark='vx'/>Angle V is thirty plus thirty, which is sixty degrees, and angle X is sixty degrees too.
<bookmark mark='uw'/>Angle U and angle W are one hundred eighty minus sixty, which is one hundred twenty degrees.

beats.on_screen: (iv) OIEA, ∠OEA = 20°: OE cuts ∠E and ∠O in half, so ∠E = ∠O = 20 + 20 = 40°; ∠A = ∠I = 180 − 40 = 140°

marks.eo: angle E and angle O are each made of two twenty degree parts
marks.ai: angles A and I are written

narration: <bookmark mark='diag'/>Step four, the diagonal O E cuts angle E and angle O in half.
<bookmark mark='eo'/>Angle E is twenty plus twenty, which is forty degrees, and angle O is forty degrees too.
<bookmark mark='ai'/>Angle eigh and angle I are one hundred eighty minus forty, which is one hundred forty degrees.

marks.chk: the four angle sums are written one below another
marks.tot: each total shows three hundred sixty
marks.tot2: the last totals show three hundred sixty

narration: <bookmark mark='chk'/>Step five, check each shape.
The four angles of every shape add up to three hundred sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='tot'/>Forty plus one hundred forty, twice over, is three hundred sixty.
One hundred ten plus seventy, twice over, is also three hundred sixty.
<bookmark mark='tot2'/>Sixty plus one hundred twenty, twice over, is three hundred sixty as well.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Each shape has two pairs of equal angles.
In the first shape, angles E and R are one hundred forty degrees, and angle eigh is forty.
<bookmark mark='a2'/>In the second, angles Q and S are seventy degrees.
Angle R is one hundred ten.
<bookmark mark='a3'/>In the third, angles V and X are sixty degrees.
Angles U and W are one hundred twenty.
<bookmark mark='a4'/>In the fourth, angles E and O are forty degrees.
Angles eigh and I are one hundred forty.
